Tu Youyou

Pharmacology · China · b. 1930

3 min read2 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected 2 timesUpdated 20 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

Project 523 was a secret military programme with more than five hundred scientists in it. In 2015 the Nobel committee gave its prize to one of them.

If you keep one line

The recipe said do not boil it. Everything after that line was chemistry.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

The project took its name from the date of its founding meeting in Beijing: 23 May 1967. It was secret, and its short-term goal was antimalarial drugs that could be used on the battlefield. Vietnamese soldiers fighting the United States were being disabled by malaria that chloroquine no longer cured. More than five hundred scientists from some sixty institutions were drawn in. Tu Youyou joined in January 1969, to lead a group screening traditional Chinese remedies. She had trained in pharmacy at Beijing Medical College, graduating in 1955. She had no doctorate. Her group collected more than two thousand recipes and tested 380 extracts on infected mice.

The lead that held came from Ge Hong's handbook of emergency prescriptions, written around 340. In Louis Miller and Xinzhuan Su's translation it says to "take one bunch of Qinghao, soak in two sheng (~0.4 liters) of water, wring it out to obtain the juice and ingest it in its entirety." Soaked, not boiled. Tu reasoned that heat was destroying whatever worked, and switched to ether at low temperature. In October 1971 the ether extract, sample 191, cleared the parasite in mice. In July 1972 she and two colleagues took the first doses themselves, in hospital, before anyone gave it to a patient. Pure crystals followed that year, from her group and from others using her method.

The popular version credits traditional medicine with the drug. Ge Hong supplied one procedural clue: do not heat it. The switch to ether, the isolation, the structure and the 1973 derivative dihydroartemisinin were twentieth-century pharmaceutical chemistry. Tu titled her Nobel lecture "Artemisinin — A Gift from Traditional Chinese Medicine to the World" all the same. She shared the 2015 prize with William Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura, and Chinese coverage fixed on her "three nos": no doctorate, no study abroad, no seat in a national academy. Nor is the drug a finished story. In January 2025 the World Health Organization confirmed partial resistance to artemisinin in the Greater Mekong and in Eritrea, Rwanda, Uganda and Tanzania.

02Where it is contested

Who found it is the argument, and it was argued in public in China. The Lasker award in 2011 and the Nobel in 2015 both went to one person from a programme of more than five hundred. Zhang Jianfang, a former deputy director of the project, called the result a collective achievement that no individual could have produced under its conditions. Zhang Daqing and Li Runhong, historians at Peking University, pressed a subtler point: Tu was a director assigned a task by the state, not a principal investigator running her own programme, so the Western way of allocating credit does not fit how the work was organised. The case for Tu rests largely on Louis Miller and Xinzhuan Su, who began investigating in 2007 and wrote in Cell that their findings "left no doubt that the major credit must go to Youyou Tu." Their method was mostly interviews. It is fair to say that is thin for the weight two prize committees put on it. It is also fair to say the critics have not named a better candidate; on Miller and Su's account the crystals made by Luo Zeyuan in Yunnan and the clinical work of Li Guoqiao both built on her method.

03Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 9 · Sept 2026 · Six lives said more than their sources.

A sourcing pass opened the documents behind the figures in eight lives, and six said more than those documents do. Fritz Haber said roughly half the nitrogen in your body came through his process and that three to four billion people are alive because of it. The first line was found in no document opened. The study most often cited gives 48 per cent of the world's population in 2008, and the entry now says that. John D. Rockefeller put Standard Oil's ninety per cent of American refining in the early 1880s; the source opened puts it at 1879. Andrew Carnegie called the 1901 sale the largest transaction in industrial history; neither source opened says so, and the sentence now says what they do. Robert Moses gave thirteen bridges and hundreds of playgrounds as Caro's count; only the $27 billion was found. Steve Jobs said he paid Lucasfilm for its graphics group; by Alvy Ray Smith's account the new company paid for the technology out of Jobs's ten million. Tu Youyou's sixty laboratories are sixty institutions in the WHO's count. Each figure now carries the document it was read in.

№ 16 · Sept 2026 · Five quotations the house had not seen.

An audit of quotations checked each one against the document it comes from. Five could not be found in any document the house could open, so they are no longer printed in quotation marks: Confucius on not imposing on others (the translator was never named), Ibn Khaldun on dynasties lasting three generations (not found in the Rosenthal translation the entry relies on), Robert Moses's 'stein' statement (two wordings circulate, and the 1981 obituary that carries it could not be opened), Clair Patterson's 1966 testimony about the Public Health Service, and Thomas Blanton's line about Arkhipov. Each is now given as a paraphrase, which is what the colophon says an unquoted line is. None of them has been shown to be wrong. Separately, Tu Youyou's entry called Rao, Zhang and Li's book the only book-length account in English; Tu's own 2017 book covers the same discovery, as chemistry rather than history.

04The definitive biography

Tu Youyou and the Discovery of Artemisinin: 2015 Nobel Laureate in Physiology or MedicineYi Rao, Daqing Zhang and Runhong Li · 2016

The book-length history of the project in English (Tu's own 2017 book, From Artemisia annua L. to Artemisinins, is a chemistry monograph), by the Peking University scholars who went through the project's records and interviewed its members. It is short, nationalistic in places and has almost no references (Anthony Dayan's review says so plainly), so read it with Miller and Su's four-page 'Artemisinin: Discovery from the Chinese Herbal Garden' in Cell (2011). It prints her Nobel lecture in full.

05Reads across to

Norman Borlaug — the other life on this shelf credited with lives by the million. Hers is the one the house would not put a number on: no clean figure exists for artemisinin alone.

Maurice Hilleman — the vaccine-maker almost nobody can name, beside the drug-maker almost nobody can name.

Frances Kelsey — the other end of a drug's life: the reviewer who kept one off the American market by insisting the safety case be made.

Alice Ball — the same problem fifty years earlier, and the same answer: the plant was never the discovery, the extraction was.
